passages.t: They will put you out of the synagogues
passages.happening:
Jesus tells his friends why he is warning them: “I have told you these things so that you will not fall away” (verse 1).

“They will put you out of the synagogues. In fact, a time is coming when anyone who kills you will think he is offering a service to God” (verse 2). People will do this “because they have not known the Father or Me” (verse 3).

He tells them now, so that when it happens they will remember that he warned them. He did not say it at the beginning, because he was with them (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
To be put out of the synagogue was a heavy cost. The synagogue was the center of a Jewish town's life: its prayer, its reading of Scripture, its friendships, its help in hard times. To lose it could mean losing your place among your own people, even your own family.

John speaks of this three times (9:22, 12:42, 16:2). The book page and the note on 9:22 explain what historians say. Many scholars think John's book was finished in a time of painful separation, when some Jews who believed in Jesus had been put out of their synagogues. Others argue that local exclusions like this could well have happened in Jesus' own lifetime. Luke records Jesus warning of the same thing: people will ‘exclude you’ because of the Son of Man (Luke 6:22).

The warning about killing came true within a few years. Stephen was stoned (Acts 7:58-60). Saul of Tarsus, before he became the apostle Paul, says, “I too was convinced that I ought to do all I could to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth” (Acts 26:9). He describes himself as “extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers” (Galatians 1:14). He truly thought he was serving God.

The word Jesus uses for ‘service’ is the word for worship at the temple. That is what makes the warning so frightening. The people who do this will think it is an act of worship.
passages.ot: Isaiah knew this sorrow: “Your brothers who hate you and exclude you because of My name have said, ‘Let the LORD be glorified’” (Isaiah 66:5). God's answer there is that they will be put to shame, and the excluded will see joy. People who drove out the faithful while claiming to honor God are an old story in the Scriptures.
passages.hard:
‘Whoever kills you will think he is offering a service to God’ is not a charge against the Jewish people. Jesus and all eleven friends listening to him were Jews. Many of the first believers were Jews, and so was Saul, who acted on that zeal before he met Jesus. The warning is about what religious zeal can do in any people who think God is on their side.

And Christians have done this very thing. Christians have killed Jews and thought they served God, as crusaders did when they massacred the Jewish communities of Worms and Mainz in 1096. Christians have killed other Christians and thought they served God, as when the Protestant authorities of Zurich drowned the Anabaptist Felix Manz in 1527 for baptizing adults. This verse warns the church as much as anyone. It gives no one, ever, leave to hate or hurt another person in God's name.
passages.asks: Jesus warned his friends ahead of time so that trouble would not knock their faith over. Ask whether you expected following Jesus to be easy. And if you have been hurt by religious people who were sure they were doing God's work, perhaps even in a church, notice that Jesus saw it coming and named it. He stands with the one who is pushed out, not with the one who pushes.

passages.t: It is for your benefit that I am going away
passages.happening:
“Now, however, I am going to Him who sent Me; yet none of you asks Me, ‘Where are You going?’” (verse 5). Instead, sorrow has filled their hearts (verse 6).

“But I tell you the truth, it is for your benefit that I am going away. Unless I go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send Him to you” (verse 7).

When the Advocate comes, “He will convict the world in regard to sin and righteousness and judgment” (verse 8): about sin, because they do not believe in Jesus; about righteousness, because Jesus is going to the Father; and about judgment, “because the prince of this world has been condemned” (verses 9-11).
passages.hearers:
Peter asked earlier, ‘Lord, where are You going?’ (13:36), and Thomas said, ‘we do not know where You are going’ (14:5). So why does Jesus say none of them asks? Many readers think he means that they have stopped asking now. They are so full of their own sorrow at losing him that they are not thinking about where he is going: to the Father, and to glory.

‘For your benefit’ must have sounded impossible. How could losing Jesus be good for them? His answer is the Spirit. While Jesus was on earth, he was in one place at a time. The Spirit will be with every one of them, everywhere, and in them.

The Greek word behind ‘convict’, elenchō, means to bring something into the light, to show it for what it is, to prove someone wrong. It is a courtroom word. The world put Jesus on trial and found him guilty. The Spirit will turn the trial around and show the world that it was wrong: wrong about sin, because the real sin was refusing to believe in him; wrong about righteousness, because the Father raised and welcomed the one they condemned; wrong about judgment, because at the cross it was the devil who was judged.
passages.ot: The prophets promised that God would pour out his Spirit: “And afterward, I will pour out My Spirit on all people” (Joel 2:28). Isaiah said of the coming king, “The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him” (Isaiah 11:2), and that a day would come “until the Spirit is poured out upon us from on high” (Isaiah 32:15). Jesus says that this gift depends on his going away.
passages.hard: Does ‘convict the world’ mean the Spirit makes people feel guilty? Not mainly. The word is about exposing what is true, not about producing a feeling. When the Spirit shows a person their sin, the purpose is to bring them to Jesus, not to crush them. Many Christians can tell of a time when they saw, perhaps suddenly, that they had been wrong about Jesus. That is the work this verse describes. Guilt that only drives a person to despair, with no way back to God, is not what Jesus is describing here.
passages.asks: The disciples were so full of sorrow that they could not see what Jesus was giving them. Ask whether there is a loss in your life that you can only see as loss. Jesus does not say their sorrow was foolish. He says there is more going on than they can see. Ask him to show you what he may be doing in it.

passages.t: He will guide you into all truth
passages.happening:
“I still have much to tell you, but you cannot yet bear to hear it” (verse 12).

“However, when the Spirit of truth comes, He will guide you into all truth. For He will not speak on His own, but He will speak what He hears, and He will declare to you what is to come” (verse 13).

The Spirit will glorify Jesus, by taking what belongs to Jesus and making it known to them. And everything that belongs to the Father belongs to Jesus (verses 14-15).
passages.hearers:
Jesus is honest about his friends' limits. There is more to say, but they cannot carry it yet. A good teacher does not pour everything out at once.

‘Guide’ is a word for leading someone along a road. The Spirit does not hand over a sealed book. He walks with them into the truth, step by step.

Notice how the Spirit is described. He does not speak on his own. He speaks what he hears. He glorifies Jesus, not himself. Christians have long used this as a test: a teaching that draws attention away from Jesus, or contradicts what he said, is not from the Spirit of truth. The New Testament says, ‘test the spirits’ (1 John 4:1).

Notice too what verse 15 says about Jesus: everything the Father has is his. And the Spirit takes what is his and makes it known. Father, Son and Spirit are spoken of together, one work, three persons.
passages.ot: The Old Testament asked how a prophet's word could be tested. The Law said that even a prophet whose sign came true was not to be followed if he said, “Let us follow other gods” (Deuteronomy 13:2-3). The Spirit who rested on God's chosen king is called “the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and fear of the LORD” (Isaiah 11:2).
passages.hard:
To whom is ‘He will guide you into all truth’ promised? Christians answer in different ways, and each has its reasons.

Many Protestant churches read it first as a promise to the apostles, the ones in the room. They hold that the Spirit kept that promise as the apostles' teaching was given and written down in the New Testament, and that the Spirit now helps believers understand Scripture rather than adding to it. The Westminster Confession, chapter 1, says that ‘nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men’.

The Catholic Church holds that the Spirit guides the whole church through the ages, in its Scriptures and its living tradition. The Second Vatican Council said in 1965 that ‘this tradition which comes from the Apostles develops in the Church with the help of the Holy Spirit’ (Dei Verbum 8). The Orthodox churches also give a central place to the church's holy tradition, guided by the Spirit.

Pentecostal and charismatic Christians affirm that the Spirit still speaks today, through gifts such as prophecy, and most of them insist that every such word must be tested by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

These notes take no side. All agree on the test the verse itself gives: the Spirit does not speak on his own, and he glorifies Jesus.
passages.asks: Jesus did not tell his friends everything at once, because they could not bear it. He is patient with what you cannot yet understand. Ask what question about God you are still carrying, and whether you can trust the Spirit of truth to lead you, step by step, rather than demanding all the answers now.

passages.t: Your grief will turn to joy
passages.happening:
“In a little while you will see Me no more, and then after a little while you will see Me” (verse 16). The disciples are puzzled. They keep asking one another what ‘a little while’ means (verses 17-18).

Jesus knows what they want to ask. “Truly, truly, I tell you, you will weep and wail while the world rejoices. You will grieve, but your grief will turn to joy” (verse 20).

“A woman has pain in childbirth because her time has come; but when she brings forth her child, she forgets her anguish because of her joy that a child has been born into the world” (verse 21). “So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take away your joy” (verse 22).

In that day they will ask the Father in his name, and the Father will give it. “Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
‘A little while’ is about three days. Jesus will die and be buried, and they will not see him. Then he will rise, and they will. When the risen Jesus showed them his hands and side, John says, “The disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord” (20:20).

Notice what Jesus does not say. He does not say, ‘Do not weep.’ He says they will weep and wail. Their grief is real, and it is right. The joy comes after the grief, not instead of it.

In the ancient world childbirth was dangerous. Many women died giving birth, and many babies did not live. Every hearer knew that. The picture Jesus uses is not of something easy. It is of real pain, real danger and real fear, that ends in a new life.

The prophets used the same picture for the hard birth of God's new age. Paul says the whole creation is groaning ‘in the pains of childbirth’, waiting (Romans 8:22).
passages.ot: The Psalms promise that grief is not the end: “Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning” (Psalm 30:5). “Those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy” (Psalm 126:5). And Isaiah uses the picture of a woman in labor: “As a woman with child about to give birth writhes and cries out in pain, so were we in Your presence, O LORD” (Isaiah 26:17). Later he promises that God will not bring a child to the point of birth and fail to deliver it (Isaiah 66:9).
passages.hard:
What about a sorrow that does not seem to turn to joy? Some griefs last for years. Jesus' words were first about three days: the cross, and then the empty tomb. For many readers the ‘little while’ has been much longer. The promise does not say that every sorrow ends quickly, or that every loss is replaced in this life. It says that Jesus will see his people again, and that the joy he gives no one can take away. The last pages of the Bible promise that God “will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). Until then, a psalm says, God keeps count of our tears (Psalm 56:8).

And some readers come to verse 21 with their own pain. For a woman who lost a baby in pregnancy or at birth, or who lost her own health, or who longs for a child and has none, a picture of a mother forgetting her anguish may hurt more than it helps. Jesus is not saying that every pain ends in a birth, or that the pain does not matter. He is using a picture everyone knew to promise his friends that their grief would not have the last word. If this is a hard verse for you, you are not wrong to feel it. Grief like that should not be carried alone. Reach out to people you trust, to a pastor, or to someone trained to help.
passages.asks: Jesus did not tell his friends to stop grieving. He told them their grief would be turned, not erased. Ask what sorrow you are carrying, and whether you have let yourself grieve it before God. And hold on to the promise at the center: ‘I will see you again.’ The joy he gives is not something the world can take.

passages.happening:
Jesus says he has been speaking in pictures, but the hour is coming when he will speak plainly about the Father (verse 25). They will ask the Father in his name, “For the Father Himself loves you, because you have loved Me and have believed that I came from God” (verse 27). “I came from the Father and entered the world. In turn, I will leave the world and go to the Father” (verse 28).

The disciples say, “See, now You are speaking plainly” (verse 29). Now they are sure he knows all things, and they believe he came from God (verse 30).

“Do you finally believe?” Jesus replies (verse 31). The hour has come when they will be scattered, each to his own home, and leave him alone. “Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me” (verse 32).

“I have told you these things so that in Me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
The disciples think they finally understand. Jesus knows that within hours they will all run away. He does not shame them for it. He tells them ahead of time, and then he gives them his last word before his prayer: peace, and courage.

‘The Father Himself loves you’ (verse 27) is worth stopping on. Jesus is not standing between them and an angry Father who must be talked into loving them. The Father loves them already.

‘Tribulation’ means trouble, pressure, hardship. Jesus does not promise his followers an easy life. He promises two things side by side: trouble in the world, and peace in him.

‘I have overcome the world’ is said the night before the cross, by a man about to be arrested, beaten and killed. He speaks as if the victory is already won. In John's book, it is. The cross is not a defeat that Easter has to undo. It is where the world's power is broken.
passages.ot:
The scattering was foretold: “Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zechariah 13:7). Mark records that Jesus quoted this very verse that night: ‘I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered’ (Mark 14:27).

And Jesus' words ‘I am not alone, because the Father is with Me’ echo the trust of the Psalms. Even when friends and family turn away, the psalmist knows that God has not: “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (Psalm 27:10).
passages.hard: If Jesus has overcome the world, why is there still so much trouble? Jesus himself says, in the same breath, that his followers will have tribulation. He does not deny the trouble. He says that it does not have the last word. The First Letter of John puts it this way: “And this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith” (1 John 5:4). The victory is real now, and it is not yet complete. Christians live between the empty tomb and the day when every tear is wiped away.
passages.asks: Jesus knew his friends would leave him alone, and he still spoke to them of peace. If you have been left alone in a crisis, he knows what that is like, and he found the Father with him. Ask where you need courage today. He does not say ‘be brave because it will not be hard’. He says: it will be hard, and I have overcome.
